beliefs.limiting: I’ve watched porn since I was a teenager. It’s wired in. I’m stuck with it.
beliefs.counterpart: Out-of-control porn use often doesn’t last. Plenty of people get past it.
beliefs.test: This week, write down one habit you were once sure you’d never drop, and did. Next to it, write what changed. Notice whether “wired in” held up.
beliefs.proof: An Israeli survey of adults asked about compulsive sex and problem porn use in 2018 and 2022. Of the groups with likely problems in 2018, 138 people fell in a ‘recovery’ group by 2022; 42 stayed ‘chronic’.

problems: Only the abstract can be read; the full text is paywalled. The figures 138 ('recovery') and 42 ('chronic') and both quotes match the abstract word for word.
'Checked adults' reads like a clinical check. The source is a community survey (Jewish adults in Israel, aged 18 to 70) using self-report measures of probable CSBD and PPU.

'Of those flagged in 2018' is inferred from the profile names. The groups come from latent profile analysis; the abstract does not say each person was over a cut-off in 2018 and under it in 2022. Use the source's own labels.

The severity tag 'disorder' fits (probable CSBD/PPU by questionnaire, mild included). Name it as weak under rule 17: a community sample, questionnaire-only, profile memberships rather than diagnoses, mixing compulsive sex with porn.
The cite's year of 2026 matches PubMed (Addictive Behaviors 175:108589). The proof is 29 words, now 37.

beliefs.limiting: Quitting means a brutal flatline and weeks of withdrawal.
beliefs.counterpart: I’ve had days off before. They weren’t brutal; the pull was the hard part.
beliefs.test: Rate your mood, sleep and focus 0–10 each night: three nights while you still watch, then each night of your first days off. Notice which nights score worse.
beliefs.proof: In a small study, 14 men who scored as hooked on sex kept off all sex, porn included, for 10 days. Their withdrawal-type symptoms eased from day 3; by day 10 they matched men below the cut-off.

problems: The groups were set by the Hebrew Bergen-Yale Sex Addiction Scale (cut-off 18). The authors say this grouping did not isolate porn-specific behaviour. 'Hooked on sex or porn' overstates the porn part.
'Men who weren't hooked' is too strong: 13 of the 16 comparison men scored in the questionnaire's 'moderate sex addiction risk' band. Say 'below the cut-off'.
The n of 14 is correct, but it is only the men who kept to the break: one man with CSB who slipped was excluded. 'Kept off' says this.

Both quotes are word for word ('3rd' is a superscript in the source). The figures hold: WSQ 63.86 at baseline, 54.36 at day 3, 33.43 at day 10, against 40.00 for non-CSB men. Israel, men recruited through social media, all male.
The severity tag 'disorder' is acceptable (a questionnaire cut-off). Small, motivated, self-selected sample; the authors themselves urge caution.

beliefs.limiting: I need it to switch off. Nothing else works at the end of the day.
beliefs.counterpart: Porn is one way I switch off. It isn’t the only one I have.
beliefs.test: The next three times you reach for porn to switch off, do something else for 15 minutes first: a walk, a shower, a call. Rate the pull 0–10 before and after. Notice how much of the need the swap covered.
beliefs.proof: In 104 men’s quit journals, most calling themselves addicted, they had often relied on porn to handle bad moods, and bad moods seemed to have become a trigger. Their own accounts, not a trial.

beliefs.limiting: I slipped again. I’m just someone who can’t quit.
beliefs.counterpart: A slip is one day. The days I kept still happened.
beliefs.test: If you slip this week, write down that night what came just before it. Then count the days you kept this month. Notice whether the slip deleted any of them.
beliefs.proof: Of 104 men journaling a porn quit, most calling themselves addicted, 55 slipped at least once. The researchers’ reading: quitting is hard, and doable with the right mix of support and habits. Men’s own accounts, not a trial.

do: Write down what porn does for you: stress relief, sleep, boredom, loneliness.
Each one is a belief to test. Start with the table above.
Don’t quit yet. For the next few days, watch the way you normally do.
Before each time, write one line: the hour, where you are, what you felt just before.
After, one more line: what it gave you, and what it cost.
At the end, circle what repeats. Those hours and feelings are what your swaps are for.

proof.text: In a 10-week diary study of 9 men in treatment in Poland, 6 binged. For most of the 6, binge days came with low mood, stress or anxiety; which one differed from man to man.

ref.cite: Wordecha M, Wilk M, Kowalewska E, Skorko M, Łapiński A, Gola M (2018). “Pornographic binges” as a key characteristic of males seeking treatment for compulsive sexual behaviors: qualitative and quantitative 10-week-long diary assessment. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 7:433-444.
ref.quote: diary assessment data indicate that specific correlates of binge PuM (decreased mood, increased stress, and anxiety) differ between subjects

problems: Wrong n for the finding: only 6 of the 9 men binged, and the mood, stress and anxiety comparisons (Table 5) cover those 6. Of them, 5 showed a significant difference; patient G showed none. So 'binges came with' holds for most of the 6, not all 9.
'Seeking help': they were patients in treatment for CSB at sexual-health centres in Warsaw, Poland, each meeting at least 4 of Kafka's 5 criteria.
The quote is word for word from the abstract. Correlation only; the authors say the causal relation is undetermined.

do: Late nights: the phone charges outside the bedroom.
Stress or boredom: a walk, a workout, a call with a friend.
Loneliness: put that energy into meeting real people.
A craving that won’t let go: a cold shower, then out of the room.
The laptop lives on a desk or a shared table, never in bed.
A swap only has to cover 80% of the need. It doesn’t have to feel as good.

do: Install a blocker and give the password to someone else.
Start with a 7-day break as an experiment.
Put that first day a few days or weeks out, not tonight, and tell one person the date.
After the week, keep going: for three months, porn is the one thing. Leave the rest of your life as it is.
Mark every kept day. Each one is a complete success, whatever else went wrong.
Slip? Write down what came just before it, then go back to step 1.

do: If shame is the engine, work on your values, not only the habit.
A slip is information, not proof you’re broken.
When the urge comes, name it: “there is a craving.” Not “I want to.” Never “I need to.”
Don’t fight the thought. Let the craving sit there and carry on with what you were doing.
When it pulls, answer the way a man who doesn’t watch porn would: “I don’t watch that.”
Count the evenings you get back, not the days you missed.

do: Look for a therapist who uses CBT or ACT.
Help is a tool for steps 1 to 4, not a replacement for them.
Embarrassed to ask? A therapist who works with this has heard it all before.
Try a group, online or in a room. Go a few times, and keep going only while it helps.
Don’t wait for a pill. None is proven for porn yet.

proof.text: In one small US trial of 28 men, nearly all Latter-day Saints, self-reported viewing fell 93% after 12 sessions of ACT, against 21% on the waiting list.

problems: The figures and the quote match the abstract word for word (93% ACT against 21% waitlist; 12 sessions; 28 adult males). Full text is paywalled; the USU dissertation copy sits behind a Cloudflare check.
A key caveat is missing: all but 1 of the 28 were Latter-day Saints, and viewing was self-reported.
